blocks.text: Why I Created an Open Atlas of the LLM Inference Ecosystem
Over the last few months, I have been writing this LLM Inference Challenges series to understand how modern inference systems work.
We started with concepts like KV cache, batching, GPU utilization, distributed inference, vLLM, llama.cpp, llm-d, routing, and many other topics.
One thing I noticed while learning was that understanding the concepts was only half the challenge.
The other half was simply keeping up.
Every week, I would come across:

a new inference engine
a new serving framework
another optimization paper
a new benchmark
another routing project
a model release
a hardware announcement
or an interesting blog explaining something I hadn't seen before.
The pace of innovation in this space is incredible.
It is also overwhelming.
After a while, I found myself asking the same question repeatedly:
"Where did I see that project?"
or
"What category does this tool belong to?"
or
"How does this fit into everything else?"
That question eventually became Inference Atlas.
What is Inference Atlas?
Inference Atlas is an open-source, community-driven directory of the LLM inference ecosystem.
GitHub: https://github.com/aruanurag/inference-atlas
Website: https://www.inferenceatlas.org/
The goal is intentionally simple.
Instead of trying to become another benchmark or another search engine, I wanted one place where I could quickly understand:

what a project does
where it fits in the inference stack
why it exists
and what related projects I should explore next.
Think of it as a map rather than a ranking.
Why build another directory?
There are already many excellent resources.
The problem isn't that information doesn't exist.
The problem is that it is scattered.
One day I am reading:
a GitHub repository
The next day:
a research paper
Then:
an NVIDIA blog
Then:
a LinkedIn post
Then:
documentation
Then:
a conference talk
After a few weeks, I realized I was spending more time trying to remember where something lived than actually learning it.
Inference Atlas became my way of organizing that knowledge.
The ecosystem is much larger than I expected
When I first started this series, I thought LLM inference mostly meant running a model.
Now I see an ecosystem that spans many layers.
For example:
Inference Engines

vLLM
llama.cpp
TensorRT-LLM
SGLang
TGI
Serving & Distributed Inference

llm-d
Ray Serve
Kubernetes-based serving
Model routers
Optimization

Continuous batching
PagedAttention
Speculative decoding
Prefix caching
Quantization
Hardware

CPUs
GPUs
NPUs
AI accelerators
Observability

Metrics
Benchmarking
Profiling
Monitoring
Model Formats

GGUF
Safetensors
ONNX
TensorRT engines
And that's only a small part of it.
Every week, new projects appear.
Keeping track of all of them has become a challenge in itself.
Why call it an Atlas?
An atlas doesn't try to tell you where to go.
It simply helps you understand the landscape.
That is exactly what I wanted.
I don't want Inference Atlas to say:
"This is the best project."
Instead, I want it to answer:

What problem does this solve?
Where does it fit?
What should I learn next?
What are similar projects?
Sometimes, simply knowing that a project exists is enough to start learning.
Built for learners first
Although anyone can use it, I built it primarily for people like me.
People who are trying to understand LLM inference one concept at a time.
If you've followed this series, you'll know I like building mental models.
Inference Atlas follows the same philosophy.
Instead of remembering hundreds of project names, I want to understand how they connect.
It will keep evolving
This isn't meant to be a static website.
As the ecosystem evolves, the Atlas should evolve too.
Some categories will grow.
Some projects will disappear.
New inference techniques will emerge.
That is completely expected.
In many ways, the Atlas is another learning project.
As I learn, it grows.
This is where I need your help
One of the reasons I made the project open source is because there is no way one person can keep up with everything happening in LLM inference.
If you know about:

an interesting inference project
a serving framework
an optimization library
a benchmarking tool
a deployment platform
a useful paper
or anything else that belongs in this ecosystem,
I would love your help.
You can:

⭐ Star the repository
Fork it and submit a Pull Request
Open a GitHub Issue with enough context for me to review and add it
My hope is that over time this becomes something the community helps build together.
Why this fits into the series
Although this article is a little different from the previous ones, I think it belongs here.
Learning LLM inference is no longer just about understanding transformers or GPUs.
It is also about navigating a rapidly evolving ecosystem.
Inference Atlas is my attempt to make that journey a little easier—for myself first, and hopefully for others too.
If it saves someone an hour of searching, or helps them discover a project they wouldn't have found otherwise, then it has already done its job.
